7. Settle on one display voice. The H1 is a bold grotesque, while every other heading (The same numbers, Point your agent here, The Methods) and the Q are a high-contrast serif. They are hard to read in light mode and only just legible in dark. Raise their size or contrast one step. KEEP

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED

- Identical disk/S3 figures across machines, left unexplained, invite the false conclusion that the machines perform the same on I/O (see 3).

v8.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Stop rounding the headline table by default (desktop-light-01, the line above the table: 'Rounded to four significant figures… Every digit' toggle off). The project's stance is exact figures, the hero card shows every digit, the JSON caption says 'nothing rounded', and the section is headed 'as measured'. Yet the main table, the thing most people compare, shows rounded values. Show the exact p50 by default in tabular mono, with digits past the fourth significant figure in a lighter tone if density is the worry. Then remove the toggle or flip it to 'Short form'. This fixes the page's one real contradiction at its cause.
2. Show the spread and the Run count in the table itself, not only on hover (desktop-light-01/02, every figure cell). Each cell already carries a dotted underline. Draw a thin p5–p95 whisker there, the same mark as the hero card's range bar, and add 'n=36' in the row's unit line or the column header. On phone, 'Hover a figure' does nothing (phone-light-03). Right now the table carries no sign of variance, so the trust story stops at the hero card.
3. Make the table denser and easier to compare. Rows are about 95–115 px tall on desktop because each one repeats a two-line description and a unit line. Fourteen rows take up most of two screens, and you cannot see Memory and Disk together. Put each description in a tooltip or in a single line in a lighter tone. Keep the unit and 'less/more is faster' as a small column. Mark the best figure in each row (bold or a rust dot) so the eye can scan for winners. Instances.vantage.sh shows how dense a figure table can get and still read well.
4. Say why the Disk figures are identical across all five machines (desktop-light-02, Disk group: 131.1 MB/s ×5, 333.3 µs ×5, ~900 µs ×5). These are the root EBS gp3 volume's baseline limits (125 MiB/s, 3,000 IOPS), not properties of the machines. i4i.2xlarge's local 1×1875 NVMe SSD, listed in its machine card, is never measured. Add a one-line group note ('all five read the same gp3 root volume, so these figures are its limits'). Without it, a reader or an agent will take these as machine comparisons.
5. On phone, the three curl commands look identical (phone-light-06, For agents section). Each one is cut to '$ curl https://api.ledgermath.com', so you cannot tell index, series and prices apart. On desktop the prices URL also runs under the Copy button (desktop-light-03). Wrap the command, or show the path first ('/v1/index.json', with the host in the label). Never truncate the part that tells the commands apart.
6. Phone table length (phone-light-03 to -06): 14 cards × 5 rows is roughly four tall screens of near-identical cards. Let the reader pick a machine to compare against, or use a compact 5-column grid with the machine names abbreviated in a sticky header row (m5.l / c8i.2xl …). Then a benchmark takes about 2 rows of height instead of a 400 px card. At minimum, add a jump list of the five groups at the table's top.
7. Give units one form across the machine cards (desktop-light-01, The machines). Network reads 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit', and Processor ranges from 'Intel Xeon Platinum 8175' to 'AMD EPYC 9R45 Processor'. If these are AWS's own strings, say so in the section caption. Otherwise put every network figure in Gbps and drop the repeated 'Processor'. The cards are also tall for five facts each: they could be a compact five-column spec table that lines up with the headline table's columns, which already carry vCPU and price.
8. Clear up the gap between the run schedule and the clock (desktop-light-00, middle stat). Boots happen at 04:10/10:10/16:10/22:10, yet the 'newest Run' is 17:07. Add 'Runs follow each boot one after another' or show the boot time beside the newest Run. Also say what the dial is: it reads as a 24-hour dial only once you notice the '00' and '12' labels.

KEEP
- The hero's split: a plain claim headline on the left and 'One figure, traced to its source' on the right. The card carries the exact digits, a correctly scaled p5/p50/p95 bar, counted and failed Runs, the date span, the setting, the Method, the zone and price, and the Series URL. It is the best single statement of what the project is, and it reads well on phone and in dark mode.
- The 'Newest Run started…' line under the CTAs, and the footer's nanosecond snapshot timestamp.
- The dark agent section: curl plus Copy, a one-line 'what you get' under each command, schema links, and the real JSON excerpt of the very Series shown at the top, with the 'nothing rounded' caption. The excerpt closing the loop with the hero is excellent.
- The 'A Method, versioned and written down' section, which quotes the definitions (R type 7 and so on) verbatim. Rare, and right for this audience.
- Plain-English benchmark names with a one-sentence description, an explicit unit and a 'less/more is faster' cue. The column headers carry vCPU and $/h.
- The type system (serif display, sans body, mono for identifiers) and a warm palette whose dark mode is done properly rather than inverted.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- 'Rounded to four significant figures' under a heading that says 'as measured', on a page whose JSON caption says 'nothing rounded'. See change 1.
- 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes', which is a count or rate, but the figure is 'µs per repetition, less is faster'. Make the description and the unit agree. 'Sort 1 MiB… How fast one core copies and sorts' against a time unit is a milder version of the same slip.
- The identical Disk figures look like machine results but are the volume's limits (change 4).
- The mutex footnote ('the decimal point moved four places') is accurate but reads like an admission that the figure was edited. Define the unit instead: ns per critical section, from 10,000 per repetition.

Keep

Keep the Run-count links beside each figure. Keep the disk and S3 marginal notes exactly where the comparison happens; the shared gp3 explanation makes five nearly identical sequential-read results intelligible. ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The best of the set at turning figures into the pitch. A plain claim ('search every byte'), a small architecture diagram, a scale line (1T+ documents, 10M+ writes/s), then a working cost calculator and p50/p90/p99 bars for warm and cold namespaces, with the workload stated and the benchmark repo linked, plus a limits table that gives 'seen in prod' next to each limit. The dark-to-light bands, pixel-shadowed boxes and mono type are carried through with care. On phone it reflows well, though the limits table wraps awkwardly. A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. In this headless capture everything below the first section is blank (scroll-triggered content never appeared), so most of the page's length was empty: in practice it is a polished template with not enough said.

v1.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Make the table rows shorter (desktop-light-00 and -01, every row). Each row is about 130 px tall because the left column holds the title, the description and the italic spec line ('Bytes per second. 1 GiB, one thread, AVX2 loads, static build.'). The five figure cells use only the top ~60 px of that, so the 14x5 ledger runs to about 2.5 desktop screens with a band of empty space under every row of numbers. Keep the title and one line of description, and put the spec line behind a disclosure or into the Series file. Aim for about 70 px a row, so a whole section fits on one screen and the eye can move down a column. The same fix shortens the phone page.
2. Help the reader compare across a row without adding any computed figure. Today, picking the winner of a row means reading five 15-digit numbers. The rule bars are drawn from zero, so the rows where the machines are nearly equal (10, 12, 13, 14) show five identical bars and say nothing. Mark the best cell in each row according to its direction (a small mark, or keep the 'ink' weight for the leader only), and think about scaling each bar to the row's own min-max rather than from zero. The direction note '↑ higher is better' is small grey italic under the unit; it carries a lot of weight for its size.
3. Give the masthead (desktop-light-00 top, phone-light-00 top) one statement at display size before the paragraph. Right now the wordmark and tagline are followed by five lines of body text all in one weight, and the reader has to dig out what this is from it: measured AWS performance, every Run kept, static JSON for agents. 'A book of record for cloud servers' is a good line but it is poetic; a newcomer needs the plain sentence above the fold too. The metadata block on the right (newest Run, Runs, boot times) is excellent; keep it.
4. Typeset the pencil digits as a fixed grid. Group the digits by three from the decimal point and give the tail a fixed width in tabular figures, so that every median in a column lines up on its decimal point. Today the tails end ragged ('016 3', '312 7', '016 25' next to '877'), and in some rows the bold part is indented to line up while in others it is not (row 14 compared with row 10). An exact figure is the whole point of the page, so its alignment should be faultless.
5. Repeat the machine header, with price and vCPU, while scrolling (desktop). The small mono machine names repeated at each section break are good, but once you are past the first screen nothing tells you which column costs $0.096 and which costs $1.36, and price is half of any decision this page serves. If the header is already sticky, ignore this; a static screenshot cannot show it.
6. Phone (phone-light-00 to -07): the cards are properly designed, but the page is about 15 screens long and the ledger alone is about 10. Add a compact mode (hide descriptions and spec lines), or a sticky jump bar for the five sections. The curl command breaks over three lines ('$ curl / https://api.ledgermath.com/v1/ / index.json'), so it reads as three commands; let it scroll sideways on one line, or show the short address and let COPY carry the full command.
7. Give the oxblood red one job. It is used at once for section labels, the N.B. notes, the left rule of the code blocks, the double rule beside the figure column on phone and the border of the sample Run. Red italic N.B. text reads as an error or a warning, when these notes are explanations (the EBS throughput limit, the IOPS limit). Set the N.B. text in ink and keep only a red marker. In dark mode the salmon is fine, but the same overuse applies.
8. In 'For agents and developers', the 'One Run, as its Series' file gives it' panel is a list of fields annotated in prose, not JSON anyone could copy. Next to it, show a short excerpt of a real index.json or Series response, as monospace JSON with a COPY button, and say what the request returns (size, how often it changes). The four curl rows are already very good.

KEEP
The ledger idea, carried right through: three places in ink and the rest in pencil, roman-numeral sections, double rules, N.B. notes, the colophon naming the faces. It is the most distinctive point of view among the pages I calibrated against, and none of it reads as a template. Keep the 'N Runs ↗' link in every cell that opens the evidence, the honest N.B. notes on the rows limited by EBS and S3, the price and vCPU in the column headers, the AWS price quoted in AWS's own words, the 'How a figure is kept' glossary with Series 187, Runs 6,335, counted 6,335 and failed 0, and oldest and newest Run to the nanosecond. Keep the copyable curl in the first screen with 'How agents read it ↓', the four documented endpoints, and the evidence URL pattern. On phone, keep the card per benchmark with a mini-table per machine; it is a real redesign, not the desktop page squeezed. The dark mode is faithful to the light one.

FALSE OR MISLEADING
- Row 12 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight': the description says 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes', which is a count or rate, but the figure is µs per completed read, lower is better. The N.B. says this, but the description contradicts it. Rewrite it as a time.
- The masthead says each figure is printed 'to every digit', and the project does not round, yet the p5-p95 range under every figure is rounded to three places (the footnote admits it). Either print the ranges exactly as well, or say 'range rounded' where the range is shown, not only in a footnote below the table.
- The masthead's '6,335 in 187 Series' sits above a table of 70 Series whose cells show about 33 to 36 Runs each. That is reconciled only in the footnote. Say 'this table: 70 of 187 Series' near the ledger heading.
- Rows 06 ('How fast one core copies and sorts') and 01 to 04 ('How fast...') are fine. Row 10 says 'Bytes per second' while the unit is MB/s. That is consistent, but a reader may wonder whether MB means 10^6 or 2^20; say which.

v2.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Make cross-machine comparison visible, not something you have to read for. In every DATA row (desktop-light-00/01, phone-light-01..05) all five figures look the same weight, so finding the best machine for a benchmark means reading 5 long numbers. Mark the best figure in each row (and maybe the worst) with one quiet device: the accent colour on the bold digits, a small marker, or a hairline bar under each figure scaled to the row. That fixes the cause; at present the table is a very good record and a weak comparison tool.
2. Put a figure in the first screen. On desktop (desktop-light-00, top 900 px) the first row of numbers sits exactly on the fold at y~870; on phone (phone-light-00, top 1688 px) there is not one benchmark figure on the first screen. Tighten the space above DATA (the DATA intro paragraph and the jump-link row can be shorter, and STATUS could be two lines) so at least the whole MEMORY first row shows on desktop, and on phone lead with one row of real figures before or right after SYNOPSIS.
3. Give DATA the hierarchy it deserves. NAME, SYNOPSIS, STATUS, DATA, SEE ALSO are all the same small bold caps; DATA is the reason the page exists and reads as one section among ten. Keep the man-page labels but let the benchmark groups and the machine column header carry more weight. The machine header repeated above COMPUTE, OS, DISK and NETWORK is tiny pale grey (desktop-light-00 y~1435, -01 y~587, y~1223) and is hard to read; make it the same style as the top header (name + vCPU/GiB + $/h), or make that header sticky.
4. Cut the prose between the figures. Each benchmark carries a title, a description, an italic 'one repetition' line and a 'setting' line before its numbers (two or three lines on desktop, four to six on phone, e.g. phone-light-02 'Lock and unlock a mutex'). Keep the title and the one-line description visible; move 'one repetition' and 'setting' behind [+] with the exact digits. That alone would shorten the phone page by perhaps a third and let the figures dominate.
5. Make ranges consistent and the links visible. p5-p95 precision varies within a row: 'Read a file sequentially' shows 131.27-131.33 next to 131.1-131.2; 'Hash 64 bytes' shows 101.1-101.4 next to 76.64-77.18. Pick one rule (same significant digits as the bold part of the p50) and keep trailing zeros. Also, the text says 'each figure links to its Series file' but the figures carry no link affordance at all in the shots; give them a faint underline or a dotted rule so the evidence link is discoverable.
6. Fix the phone STATUS order. On phone-light-00 the three desktop columns are flattened row by row, so it reads newest, where, runs, oldest, series, schedule, prices... newest and oldest are separated, and wraps like 'UTC' alone on a line and '0 / failed' are awkward. Reorder for one column (newest, oldest, runs, series, schedule, prices, where, methods, evidence) and drop the fractional seconds on phone or let them sit in grey on the same line.
7. Show what an agent gets back. SYNOPSIS gives the three curl commands with copy buttons, which is excellent, but nowhere does the page show a few lines of the JSON a Series file returns (a figure, its n, its p5/p95, the Run link). A 6-10 line excerpt under SYNOPSIS or in FILES would make 'cite the file behind each number' concrete. Also the third command hard-codes prices/2026-11-19.json, which goes stale tomorrow; offer a stable 'latest' address if the API has one, or say the date changes daily.
8. Lift the small greys. 'p5-p95 n' labels, range text, 'n=34' and the repeated machine headers are ~11 px mid-grey on cream; they are likely below comfortable contrast, especially the light-mode range lines. Darken them a step in light mode; the dark mode is already better here.

KEEP. The man-page concept (LEDGERMATH(5), NAME/SYNOPSIS/STATUS/EXIT STATUS/FILES/SEE ALSO) is a genuine point of view, apt for a data format and its developer readers, and it is carried through to the footer; 'EXIT STATUS: 0 Runs failed of 6,335' is a lovely touch. Bold leading digits with the full exact tail in grey is the right answer to 'never round' and should stay. Decimal-aligned figures, the unit and higher/lower arrow at the start of each row, n per cell, the p50 header with vCPU/GiB/$/h per machine. STATUS (newest/oldest to the nanosecond, runs kept/counted/failed, schedule, zone, '187, 70 of them in DATA below') is honest and dense without clutter. The DISK note that these rows measure the EBS root volume, not the i4i instance store, is exactly the kind of candour that builds trust. METHODS spelled out in full (R type 7, what 'counted' means). The phone curl commands wrapped with a trailing backslash, and the phone machine cards. Both colour modes are warm and coherent.

FALSE OR MISLEADING. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes' but the figure is in microseconds, lower is better (333.3 us): the description promises a count/rate and the number is a time per completed read. Say 'the time per completed read' or show IOPS. 'Every digit printed' sits above ranges that are rounded to four or five digits; the [+] exact explanation covers it, but the sentence should say the p50 is printed in full and the ranges are shortened. The METHODS 'counted' paragraph cites 'scripts/check-events.py' and '--quick stream' with no link or explanation, which reads as internal repository jargon to a visitor. The page header 'LedgerMath Data API' presents the home page as the API's page; minor, but the API is one part of what the page offers.

v3.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Stop showing the same 70 medians three times. Table 1 (rounded p50, desktop-light-00), Figure 1 (the same p50s again plus p5/p95/n, desktop-light-01) and Table S1 (exact, desktop-light-03/04) are one dataset printed three ways, and they make up most of a desktop page of roughly 8,000 px. Merge Table 1 and Figure 1 into one table: each cell holds the median, a small 5-95 range mark and n, so it can be scanned and compared without hunting for the spread in a separate figure. Keep S1 as the full-precision appendix, or drop it once the main table is exact (see 2).
2. Resolve the conflict with the project's stance on exactness. The project does not round, yet the headline table and the figure round to four significant digits. Exact digits appear only in the abstract's one example and in S1, which is collapsed on the phone. Show every digit in the main table instead, grouped in threes as S1 already does well, with the leading significant digits in full weight and the tail lighter and smaller. That keeps the table exact and still scannable, and it removes the need for the rounding disclaimers that now fill three captions and §4.3.
3. Figure 1's caption says it shows "the spread", but on linear axes that start at zero the 5th-95th bars are invisible or a few pixels wide in most panels (a, b, e, g, j, l, n), so the figure actually shows magnitude. Either call it a magnitude comparison, or show spread so it can be seen: for example the p5-p95 width as a percentage of the median, or a zoomed axis per panel. The zero-based bars also show five identical ticks for j and l. Say on the row itself why all machines read 131 MB/s and 333 µs (the same gp3 root volume) instead of leaving that to footnote b.
4. The masthead (desktop-light-00 top, phone-light-00 top) has no way out: no Docs, no API, no source repository, though this is an open-source developer tool. The docs link appears only as Reference [6] near the bottom. Add a short nav (API · Docs · Source · Methods) to the right of the snapshot date.
5. Clean up the reference apparatus and tighten the hero. The machine list puts five identical superscript 1s after the names, and then a different "note 1" (Notes, desktop-light-03) is cited from §4.1. Table notes a-c and references [1]-[6] add two more systems. Number the notes uniquely and replace the five 1s with a plain region line. The hero (title, italic subtitle, machine list, footnote, freshness strip) uses about 330 px, so on desktop Table 1's first row sits exactly at the 900 px fold. Trim it so at least four rows of figures show on the first screen.
6. Phone: Listing 1 (phone-light-04) soft-wraps long JSON lines to column 0. It breaks the URL mid-id ("a0faf4326 / dd7.json") and wrecks the indentation, which is the one place an agent developer looks for structure. Give the block horizontal scroll, or show a trimmed listing on narrow screens. The phone page is also about 12,000 CSS px long. Collapse §4.4-4.5 (equations, the long counted-rule quote), Notes and References behind disclosures the way S1 already is.
7. Table 2's "AWS's description" column (desktop-light-01/02, and the italic line on each phone card) repeats the price word for word on every row. One sentence saying prices are printed as AWS's file words them [3] does the same job. In §4 on desktop (desktop-light-02/03, 4.1-4.3) narrow justified columns open rivers ("This snapshot holds 187 Series and 6,335 Runs: 6,335"). Set them ragged-right.
8. Table 1's columns are ragged. Decimal alignment combined with four significant digits makes the decimal point move around (column 1 of row f, "3297", hangs left of the others, and column b drifts), and a dotted underline under every one of the 70 cells adds texture that competes with the digits. Use a fixed precision per row so each column right-aligns cleanly, and show the link affordance only on hover or focus.

WHAT IS STRONG AND MUST BE KEPT
- The data-report point of view. It is carried all the way through (abstract, numbered sections, Listing, References, colophon naming the typefaces), it is unlike every reference, and it fits a project whose claim is rigour. STIX Two Text with IBM Plex Mono is a good pairing.
- The freshness strip under the title (First Run, Latest Run, Prices copied, Runs 6,335 counted, 0 failed), and on the phone the same strip as a definition list.
- The Data availability box on the first screen, with a copyable curl to index.json and the two main files beside it.
- The abstract's one exact example tied to its Series id and its count of Runs.
- Listing 1. The highlighted "p50" that maps Table 1's first figure to a JSON path is the best agent-facing detail on any of these pages. Keep Table 3 with its schema links too.
- §4: the published equations, the counted-rule quoted word for word, and the Series ids beside every exact figure in S1. S1's digit grouping in thin-space threes.
- The phone adaptations are real design, not squeezing: Table 1 is replaced by the panels, Table 2 becomes cards, Table 3 becomes a stacked list, and S1 is collapsed.
- The warm dark mode, which keeps the same hierarchy, and the restrained use of a single accent.

ANYTHING FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- Note 3 says "Nothing on this page is averaged or computed from the figures", yet Table 1 and Figure 1 round every figure. That is disclosed, but the sentence overclaims. Rounding is computation, and it sits against the project's rule of no rounding.
- Figure 1 is captioned as showing spread while it mostly cannot show it (item 3).
- The hero says machines are booted at 04:10, 10:10, 16:10 and 22:10 UTC and the benchmarks run "while it is freshly booted". The Run times shown are 1 to 3.5 hours after the nearest boot (First Run 23:36, Latest Run 17:07, and Listing 1's oldest_run_started_at 13:44:51). A careful reader will ask what "freshly" means. Explain the gap on the page, or check the data.
- Two different footnotes are both numbered 1 (item 5), so a reader following a superscript can land on the wrong one.
- The rotated vertical stamp in the left margin is borrowed from the look of preprint servers. That is fine as a genre sign but not original, and on the first screen it reads as decoration.

v4.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Give the flip clock's space to the figures (desktop-light-00, right half of the hero; phone-light-00, the dark panel under the stats). On desktop the first 900 px hold no measured figure at all: the board's column headers appear at about y=790 and the first value at about y=950. Almost all of that space goes to one fact, the time the newest Run started, shown three times (the flip digits, the nanosecond timestamp, the green 'Newest Run 17:07:23' tag on the timeline). On the phone the same fact is shown a fourth time: the pill under the headline already says 'Newest Run 17:07 UTC', then about 550 CSS px of panel repeat it. Shrink the clock to a compact strip (newest Run, the four round times, the prices link) and use the space you gain for a live slice of the board: one row with all five machines, or the five machine headers with their prices and one figure each. The page's argument is its numbers, and a visitor should see one before scrolling.
2. Demote the per-cell time chips (all board rows, desktop-light-00/01). Each cell stacks five lines, and after the big figure its heaviest mark is a solid black '16:22' chip. There are 70 of them, nearly identical, and they shout louder than the p5-p95 range, which carries more information but sits in the faintest, smallest grey type on the page. Make the time plain secondary text, or state the range once per column ('newest Runs 16:12-16:23'), and raise the p5-p95 line's size and contrast. The cell would then read: figure, every digit, spread, Runs.
3. Say which machine is best on each row. Bars are scaled per row and drawn identically whether the row is '▲ higher is faster' or '▼ lower is faster', so a long bar means best in MEM and worst in CPU/OS/DSK/NET. The arrow chip is there, but the eye follows the bars. Mark the best figure on each row (weight, a dot, or the category colour), or draw every bar so that longer means better. Comparison is the board's whole job.
4. Fix the wrapped ranges on the phone (phone-light-02/03/04: CPU 05, OS 07, DSK 10, DSK 12). The p5-p95 text breaks onto two lines ('553.87-' / '573.71') beside the bar, so the rows lose their rhythm. Move the range under the full-digit line, or narrow the bar so the range fits on one line.
5. Turn the legend strip above the board into a real key (desktop-light-00 y≈767, phone-light-00 bottom). '12.50 GB/s enough digits to tell the row apart · 12.502615200030773 every digit the API holds · [bar] median, and the 5th-95th percentile' is crammed into one tiny mono line and reads as noise. The same explanation is better written in the footnote under the board and in 'Rounding'. Give it a small labelled diagram of one cell (big figure, full digits, bar and whisker, Runs) placed beside the category tabs.
6. Account for the 117 Series that are not on the board. 'Series in the API 187 / 70 on the board' appears in the hero and twice more, but nothing on the page says what the other 117 are (groups? other Methods? requests v1?). A reader who has been taught to trust exact counts will notice. One sentence near the board fixes it.
7. Choose the body face deliberately. The condensed display caps and the mono are characterful and well matched, but the running sans (hero paragraph, row descriptions, the 'Behind every figure' text) looks like a wide fallback system sans and makes those passages read generic. Choose a text face that sits with the other two, and tighten the hero paragraph to about 60 characters per line.
8. Shorten the phone page where the length is not earned. After the board, the five machine cards (phone-light-05/06) take almost two full tiles to repeat specs that fit a compact five-row table with the SKU and AWS quote expandable, and the 'Behind every figure' steps take another long stack. The board earns its length; the reference material does not.

KEEP. The yellow-and-black signage point of view, carried consistently from the header to the footer: condensed caps for row titles, numbered sections, colour-coded category tabs and left rules (MEM/CPU/OS/DSK/NET), and a dark mode that is a real counterpart, not an inversion. The board's structure: an ID per row, what is measured, the unit and direction, a plain-English description, 'One repetition:' stated exactly, then per machine the shortened figure, every digit, the per-row bar with p5-p95, and the Run count. The phone transposition into one card per benchmark with machines as rows is right. The disk caveat banner ('These rows measure the volume as much as the machine') is candid and exactly what an agent's user needs. The machine cards that quote AWS's own price string with the SKU and rate code. The For Agents section: four commented curl commands with copy buttons, a real JSON excerpt whose highlighted value is traced back to board row OS 08 c8i.2xlarge, a schema table, and the versioning promise. The Method quoted word for word with the percentile formula, and the Rounding note.

FALSE / MISLEADING. (a) A big flip clock reading '17:07 UTC' looks like the current time; the small 'NEWEST RUN STARTED' label is easy to miss, and the departure-board conceit encourages the misreading. (b) DSK 12 is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes when 64 are kept submitted', which is a count or rate, but the figure is MEDIAN TIME in µs per completed read. Make the description match what is shown. (c) The JSON excerpt's Run (136.389 µs) and the Series median (136.370 µs) both display as '136.4 µs' in the caption, so it reads as though this Run is the median. Show one more digit, or say that they differ. Nothing else looked invented: the Run counts, dates, gp3 limits (about 131 MB/s, about 3,000 IOPS at QD64) and price strings agree with each other everywhere they appear.

v5.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Make the 14x5 grid comparable at a glance, not just readable (desktop-light-00 bottom to desktop-light-02 top). Every row is about 160 px tall, so the grid runs about three screens and the machine headers (m5.large ... c6i.8xlarge, with prices) scroll off after the first row; in desktop-light-01 and -02 you cannot tell which column is which without counting. Root cause: each cell stacks four lines (rounded figure, exact figure, p5/p95, counted Runs) and each row label stacks four levels of text. Fix the cause: (a) merge the rounded and exact figures into one line, with the leading significant digits in full weight and the trailing digits in a lighter tone, as the hero's 'Exact' line already does in red, so each figure appears once and stays exact; (b) put p5/p95 and the Run count on one small line; (c) move the 'One repetition: ...' sentence behind a disclosure or into the row's Series link. That should roughly halve the row height. Then make the machine header row sticky, or repeat it at each category rule (Memory/Compute/Operating system/Disk/Network).
2. Mark the best figure in each row. The direction is already stated ('Higher is faster' / 'Lower is faster'), but nothing shows which column wins, so every row means reading five 4-digit numbers. Bold the best cell, or put a thin in-cell bar on the same zero-based scale as the hero's 'The same benchmark on all five' chart. That chart is the most legible thing on the page, and the table drops its idea. On phone (phone-light-01 to -05) the same marker on the winning card would help just as much.
3. Show spread visually, not only as text. 'p5 908.5 · p95 1073.1' (Write 8 KiB durably, c8i.2xlarge) and 'p5 141.0 · p95 184.0' (mutex, c6i.8xlarge) are the interesting outliers, and they read the same as tight ones. A tiny p5-p50-p95 tick on each cell would make an unstable machine stand out.
4. Replace the two clock-time KPIs in section 02 (desktop-light-02: 'Newest Run 17:07', 'Oldest Run 23:36'). Huge time-of-day digits say little, and the oldest Run (10 Nov 23:36) sits oddly beside the hero's '11 November to 19 November' for its Series. Lead with the span and cadence ('9 days, 36 boots per machine'), with the exact timestamps as the small line, as they already are.
5. Disk rows: make the unit match the words, and name the limits. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' says 'How many direct reads ... completes' but shows µs per read. Add a bold derived line like the mutex row's '17.50 ns per critical section' only if the Derivation holds it; otherwise reword the description to 'time per completed read'. The disk note says these rows hit gp3's IOPS and throughput limits. Stating which limit each identical column shows (131.1 MB/s, 333.3 µs) would turn five identical numbers from 'is this broken?' into evidence.
6. Section 04 machines (desktop-light-03, phone-light-07): the raw AWS price-dimension paths ('/sources/0/terms/OnDemand/8D49XP...pricePerUnit/USD') wrap over two to four grey mono lines per machine and are the noisiest thing on the page. Keep the quoted AWS description, and make the path a single truncated link or a disclosure; the price file is already linked in the intro.
7. Phone code blocks: the JSON excerpts in 'From a figure to its evidence' (phone-light-06) are cut off at the right edge ('.../v1/series/a', '"evidence": "https://api.ledgermath.com/runs/202'). Either wrap them, or shorten the long values with an ellipsis so that the address you are teaching is visible. If they scroll sideways, show that they do.
8. Phone length is about 13,800 CSS px, nearly all of it the 70 cards. The card pattern (machine left, figure right, range under it) is properly designed for the width. Once change 1 shortens each card, consider collapsing each benchmark to its five main figures with the detail on tap, so the provenance and API sections are reachable without a long scroll.

KEEP.
- The first screen. 'AWS machines, measured four times a day.', the two-paragraph explanation, the copyable curl in the hero, and the 'Newest Run' / 'Boots every day, UTC' header together answer what, for whom and how fresh within seconds.
- The hero's exact line: the significant digits strong, the rest lighter, underlined and linked to its Series file. It is the best answer on the page to 'exact but readable'; spread it to the table (change 1).
- 'From a figure to its evidence, in two reads', with real JSON that matches the figures shown (p50 12502615200.030773 = 12.50 GB/s; the mutex Run's 136389 ns against 136.4 µs). That is exactly what an agent author needs, and it builds trust through consistency.
- The disk-section note explaining identical figures; the mutex row's per-critical-section line; the counted-Run count on every cell; 'Failed Runs are kept, never dropped'.
- The dark mode: the curl box inverts to a light block on black instead of vanishing, the red is lifted for contrast, and the bars invert cleanly.
- The restrained Swiss type system (one grotesk, mono only for addresses, one red accent), carried through consistently.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED.
- Section 02's 'Figure' card says 'Nothing rounded', while the large figures everywhere are rounded. The section 01 intro does say 'The large figure is rounded for display', but a skimmer meets the contradiction. Change 1 removes it at the source; otherwise reword the card to 'the published figure is exact; the large digits are a display rounding'.
- The red column highlight on m5.large carries over from the hero into the table. Because m5.large is the slowest in almost every row, red reads as 'worst/alert' rather than 'the figure featured above'. Consider a neutral highlight in the table, or drop it after the first row.
- Nothing else looks invented: the 14 benchmarks, 5 machines, counts and prices are consistent across the hero, the grid, section 02 and the JSON excerpts.

v6.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Say what the disk instruments are actually measuring. On desktop-light-01, '10 Read a file sequentially' shows ~131.1 MB/s on all five machines. Both charts are ZOOMED to six digits, so differences of 0.1% (131.09 vs 131.28) look like a ranking of machines. They are noise on top of a volume limit. Add one line to each card, e.g. 'All five sit at the root gp3 volume's 125 MiB/s cap', and drop the zoom, or keep it and mark the spread as within the cap. An agent reading these charts or the API will otherwise conclude something false. The cause is that a ZOOMED chart has no way to say 'these are equal'; build that state into the chart.
2. Fix the wording on card 12. 'The time until one direct read completes … with 64 kept submitted' reads as latency, but with 64 in flight the latency would be ~21 ms. The figure is time per completed read, i.e. inverse throughput. Say so in the subtitle and in the Every digit row label.
3. Thin out the Every digit table (desktop-light-02). 'p50 / p5 / p95 / n' is repeated in all five machine columns and 'Runs' 70 times, so the labels are a fifth of the ink. A careful reader will ask where the other 117 are and whether figures were chosen. Add one clause, e.g. '70 shown here: the default settings; the other 117 (other params/builds) are in series.json', linked.
5. Give agents a real handoff. 'Point an agent at the API' should go to a copyable prompt or an llms.txt-style block ('Start at /v1/index.json; every figure carries its Series file; cite it'). Wrap them, or show only the path under a shared base URL.

Let the unit wrap below, or shorten it to 'ns / section'. On the same phone charts, '14.43' on card 02 sits off the right edge used by the other figures.

CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST

The lede above the table says 'the bar under each is its 5th to 95th percentile', but each bar is really a track filled from zero to the median, scaled to the row's largest value, with a small p5–p95 whisker at its end. A reader who trusts the legend misreads every row. On top of that, a long bar means 'best' in the GB/s rows and 'worst' in the ns/µs rows, and nothing marks the winner. Fix the cause: state the encoding exactly ('bar: median against the row's largest; whisker: p5–p95'), and mark the best machine in each row with one quiet device (a bold figure or an accent tick), so the direction no longer depends on reading 'more is faster' / 'less is faster' in the label column. In the four Disk rows and the S3 row every bar sits pinned at the right end and carries no information. Consider a row scale that starts nearer the data, labelled as such, or drop the bar when the spread is under ~1% and say 'all within x%'.

2. Shorten the phone table by about 40% (phone-light-03..06). Each benchmark is a card with five two-line rows: machine name and number on one line, the bar alone on the next. That takes the table to roughly 6,000 CSS px and pushes 'Point your agent at the source' far down the page. Put the bar on the same line, to the right of the number, or under the number's light tail at half height. Also make the Memory/Compute/… chips sticky as a section index on phone, so the length has a way through it.

3. Show the table, not only one figure, before the fold on desktop (desktop-light-00). The hero card is excellent, but the page's main asset, 14×5 exact figures, starts about 3,000 px down, behind a stat strip and a five-step explainer. Move 'The headline table' up to sit directly under the hero, ahead of 'Why the numbers can be checked' and 'How it works', or put a three-row teaser of it at the bottom of the first screen. Developers who arrive to compare machines should not have to scroll past marketing to get there.

4. Rework the stat strip (desktop-light-00, middle band). '17:07 UTC, newest run' repeats the freshness line directly above it, and the 24-hour dial is too small to read (its '00'/'12' labels are ~8 px) and needs a legend to decode. Meanwhile '187 Series served' sits next to a table that shows 70, and the reconciliation ('Figures from 70 Series in a snapshot of 187; the others measure other settings and builds') is hidden in a footnote under the table. Either say '70 shown here of 187' in the strip, or swap that stat for one that carries more weight, such as the median count of Runs per figure (about 36).

5. Strip the internal vocabulary from the prose. Examples: 'disk_read_sequential's row' in the Disk note (the row is titled 'Read a file sequentially'); 'Counted: true, group A' in the Run example (desktop-light-03; 'group' is never explained); 'Derivation', 'R type 7'. Use the visible row titles, and explain 'group' in a word or drop it. Typeset the percentile formula in the Method section as a formula block, not as inline prose with floor brackets; at the moment it is the hardest-to-read paragraph on the page.

6. Add the open-source link (footer, nav). For a project whose whole pitch is 'check us', the only footer link is 'Font licences'. There is no repository link and no link to the benchmark source or how to add a benchmark. Put the repository in the nav next to 'Data API' and in the footer.

7. Bring the agent way in nearer the top and make it complete (desktop-light-02/03). The curl blocks with Copy buttons and the real series excerpt are very good. But the hero's 'Use the data API' is the only route to them, and the section sits after the full table. Add a one-line 'give your agent this' snippet (the index URL plus one sentence on what it holds) into or right under the hero. Say once, plainly, that the addresses are static JSON with no key and no rate limit (if true), and give the size of series.json so an agent knows whether to fetch it whole.

8. Small number details. In the Machines table, Network mixes 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit', and Storage reads '1 × 1875 NVMe SSD' with no unit. These are AWS's words, as the page says, but keep AWS's string as-is in a smaller second line and lead with a normalised value (Gbit/s, GB), so the row can be scanned. In the desktop table the figures sit left in their columns with ad-hoc padding (' 3.481' vs '14.428'); align each column on the decimal point, as the phone version already does.

STRONG, KEEP

It shows the exact median, the B/s value as stored, a correctly proportioned p5–p50–p95 strip, Runs counted and failed, the date span, the setting, the Method, the zone and price, and the Series file address. It shows trust where a claim would only assert it.

- '187 Series served' next to a table of 70 figures reads as a contradiction until the footnote is found.
